newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo C.Bank governor vows price, dinar stability.
newsitem.headline: Yugo C.Bank governor vows price, dinar stability.

text.p: Yugoslavia's newly appointed central bank governor Dusan Vlatkovic vowed to maintain tight monetary policy and keep prices and the dinar stable, Belgrade daily Politika reported on Friday.

"A restrictive monetary policy must be pursued in the coming period to the extent it does not lead to disinflation or stagnation of production," Vlatkovic was quoted as saying shortly after being named to his new post.
The central bank governorship has been vacant since May 1996.
Vlatkovic said additional measures were needed to facilitate the implementation of a strict monetary policy.
Additional measures included privatisation and rehabilitation of the ailing banking sector.
"The accumulated problems in banks and the economy are seriously limiting successful implementation of the monetary policy," he said.

Vlatkovic said the country needed an efficient banking system enjoying satisfactory credibility in the world financial community, particularly with the International Monetary Fund, World Bank and other institutions.
The problem of frozen savings also had to be resolved to restore confidence in banks and bring into the system new savings needed to finance the economy and the population.
Almost $4 billion in hard currency savings were frozen in 1991.
Vlatkovic insisted privatisation could help ease problems with public sector deficits, which will not be financed by printing new money.
The newly appointed National Bank of Yugoslavia governor also called for measures to boost hard currency reserves to ensure normal operation of the forex market.
Forex reserves can be boosted with part of the receipts raised from a sale of a 49 percent stake in the Serbian telecom company.

Nearly $1 billion from the strategic partnership deal which Telekom Srbija concluded with Italian and Greek telecom firms was channeled to the Serbian Development Fund and will be used to finance infrastructure, export-oriented industries and to kick-start idle factories.

But the country needed additional foreign funds which would start flowing in only after Belgrade normalises its relations with world financial bodies. Vlatkovic insisted that the NBY will be fully engaged in the normalisation process. -- Beti Bilandzic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
